T-cell development

 

Differential diagnostic algorithm

** Adult T cell leukemia / lymphoma is known to mimic other specific and well defined T cell lymphomas from clinical, histologic and immunophenotype perspectives; in particular, the histopathologic features of adult T cell leukemia / lymphoma can be indistinguishable from those of mycosis fungoides, angioimmunoblastic T cell lymphoma, anaplastic large cell lymphoma and T cell prolymphocytic leukemia.

Contributed by Jennifer Chapman, M.D.

Q. Differential diagnosis of lymphocytosis includes:

·       Reactive lymphocytosis

·       Polyclonal T-cell lymphocytosis associated with thymoma

·       Polyclonal B-cell lymphocytosis

·       B- and T-cell lymphoproliferative neoplasms

 

Q. Differential diagnosis of gamma delta γδ lymphomas includes (4 entities):

·       Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma (HSPTCL)

·       Primary cutaneous gamma delta lymphoma (PCGDTL)

·       Monomorphic epitheliotropic intestinal T-cell lymphoma (MEITL)

·       Large granular lymphocytic leukemia (T-LGL)

Mature T NK Leukemias

*T-PLL T-Cell Prolymphocytic Leukemia

 

(T-PLL is same in WHO-HAEM5)

·       Essential (major) diagnostic criteria

o   Peripheral blood lymphocytosis > 5 × 109/L or bone marrow infiltrate with T-PLL immunophenotype

o   Evidence of T-cell monoclonality

o   Demonstration of TCL1A (14q32) or MTCP1 (Xq28) rearrangement (desirable identification of juxtaposed TR locus, most frequently TRD) or TCL1A protein expression

·       Minor diagnostic criteria (at least one required)

o   Abnormalities involving chromosome 11 (11q22.3, ATM)

o   Abnormalities in chromosome 8: idic(8)(p11), t(8;8), trisomy 8q

o   Abnormalities in chromosome 5, 12, 13, or 22, or complex karyotype

o   Involvement of specific sites (e.g. splenomegaly, effusions)

 

Q. What is T-cell Prolymphocytic Leukemia? (T-PLL)         

 

●      Aggressive T-cell leukemia

●      Proliferation of small to medium-sized prolymphocytes with very high, rapidly rising WCC

●      Mature post-thymic T-cell phenotype → derived from helper T cells

●      (“prolymphocytic”) remains a misnomer, as the leukemic T-cells are post-thymic in origin

Q. Sites of involvement of T-cell Prolymphocytic Leukemia? (T-PLL)         

 

●      Peripheral blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and skin

●      Marked leukocytosis with rapidly rising WCC

●      Marked HSM in advanced disease

Q. How common is T-PLL?         

 

●      Rare - 2% of cases of mature lymphocytic leukemias in adults >30 years

Q. Who gets T-PLL?         

 

●      Median age 65 years

●      (Range 30-94)

●      Infrequent in <30 years

 

Q. What ethnicity group has increased risk for T-PLL?

●      Patients with ataxia telangiectasia who harbor ATM germline mutations

Q. What are the clinical features of T-PLL?

 

●      Most patients present with:

○      Hepatosplenomegaly

○      Generalized LAD

○      Cytopenias

○      Lymphocyte count >100 x 10^9 → marked leukocytosis/lymphocytosis with rapidly rising WCC → most frequent presentation, in 75%

○      Skin infiltration (20%)

○      Serous effusions (rare)

 



Q. What are the morphological PB and BM features of T-PLL? 

       

●      Small to medium-sized mature monomorphic lymphoid cells → look malignant

●      Nuclei

○      Round, oval, or markedly irregular nuclei (cerebriform variant in 5%)

○      Condensed chromatin

○      Visible nucleoli (variable)

●      Cytoplasm

○      Non-granular basophilic cytoplasm

○      Cytoplasmic protrusions or blebs

●      Diffuse infiltration pattern in the BM

 

Note: 25% of cases have small lymphocytes only with indistinct nucleoli

 

 

Q. What are the 3 variants?

 

●      The most commonly observed morphology (75% of cases) is a predominance of small to medium-sized cells with non-granular basophilic cytoplasm and round, oval, or markedly irregular nuclei with visible nucleoli.

●      Small cell – 25%

●      Cerebriform – 5% (looks like Sezary cells)


Q. What is the small cell variant of T-PLL?   

 

●      Cell size predominantly small

●      Nucleolus not visible by light microscopy

Q. What is a common morphological feature of T-PLL regardless of cell size or nuclear features?      

 

·       Regardless of nuclear morphology, a characteristic feature is basophilic cytoplasm with protrusions or blebs



Q. What tissues are involved commonly in T-PLL?

 

●      20% skin infiltration

●      Spleen → marked HSM

●      LN

●      BM

Q. What are the histological/morphological features of skin involvement by T-PLL?

 

●      Dense perivascular and periadnexal infiltrates without epidermotropism

Q. What does splenic infiltration by T-PLL look like? 

       

●      Red pulp expansion and white pulp attenuation by neoplastic cells

Q. What is the LN histology of T-PLL? 

       

 

●      Diffuse paracortical infiltration and attenuation of germinal centres (WHO5)

 

Q. What is the bone marrow histology of T-PLL?

●      Bone marrow aspirates show aggregates of neoplastic lymphoid cells, and

●      core biopsies demonstrate diffuse and interstitial infiltrates

Q. What cytochemical stain is positive in T-PLL?    

    

●      Alpha-naphthyl acetate esterase and acid phosphatase with a dot-like pattern in Golgi region

●      Note: cytochemistry is rarely used for routine diagnosis

 

Q. What are the differential diagnosis of T-PLL?

·       Mature T-cell neoplasms with leukemic presentation, such as ATLL, SS, and T-LGLL 

·       Lymphoid neoplasms with leukemic presentation, such as T- or B-ALL, HSTCL, CLL/SLL, and MCL. 

 

Q. What antigenic marker has therapeutic implications for T-PLL?

 

●      Usually CD52 positive → Alemtuzumab

●      Therapeutic breakthrough for T-PLL

Q. What is the immunophenotype of T-PLL?   

     

●      Post-thymic immunophenotype → mature T cell lymphoma derived from helper T cells

●      Positive for:

○      CD2, CD3, CD5, CD7 (no pan T marker loss)

●      Variable CD4 and CD8 expression

○      60% are CD4+, CD8-

○      25% (1/3rd) coexpress CD4 and CD8

■      Aberrant expression

■      Like an immature T cell

■      Almost unique to T-PLL

○      15% CD8+, CD4-

●      Usually CD52 positive (therapeutic marker) → Alemtuzumab

●      Membrane CD3 may be weak

●      Overexpression of TCL1

●      30% have S100 expression

●      Immature markers (CD34, TdT, CD1a) (-)

 

●      Flow: T-PLL (red) showing coexpression of CD4 and CD8 in a mature sCD3 positive population (unique to T-PLL)

 

What is the postulated cell of origin of T-PLL?  

 

●      Post-thymic mature T cell

●      Note: May arise from T cell at intermediate stage of differentiation between cortical thymocyte and mature T lymphocyte (CD4+, CD8+,CD7 strong, sCD3 weak)

 

Q. What is the status of the T-cell Antigen receptor in T-PLL?

  

●      Clonally rearranged TCR gamma AND beta

Q. What are the Cytogenetic abnormalities in T-PLL?   

 

  • Recurrent cytogenetic marker in > 80% of cases
  • inv(14)(q11q32) results in translocation of TCL1 oncogene into promoter/enhancer regions of TRA/TRD
  • Other translocations involving TCL1 or MTCP1 genes
  • Other cytogenetic abnormalities common, including del(11)(q22-23) resulting in ATM deletion and del(12)(p13) resulting in haploinsufficiency of CDKN1B
    • Complex karyotype ≥ 5 abnormalities linked to adverse outcome

 

 

●      inv(14) = the marker of T-PLL

What is the 2 most common genes involved in T-PLL rearrangements?    

 

●      TRA and TCL1 genes on Chr 14

○      80% have inv(14)(q11q32)

○      10% have t(14;14)(q11;q32)

■      TRA with TCL1A/B

■      TCL1 is a proto-oncogene

●      STAT5B mutation in 70% - adverse outcome

What mature B cell LPD may have TCL-1 mutations?

 

●      HCL,

●      Myeloid - BPDCN

 

Q. In TCL1 family–negative T-PLL, what mutation is most useful to establish the diagnosis of T-PLL?

·       Deletions and/or mutations of ATM, which are found in 80–90% of all T-PLL cases but are usually absent in other mature T-cell malignancies, are considered to best aid in establishing the diagnosis of presumed TCL1 family–negative T-PLL.

 

What is the prognosis of T-PLL?

  

●      Aggressive disease, Median survival 1-2 years

●      Note: Cases with chronic course reported, but they progress after 2-3 years

What is the best treatment for T-PLL? 

       

●      Alemtuzumab/Campath

●      Pentostatin and CHOP

●      Stem cell transplant should be considered for those in remission after immunotherapy

What is the Alemtuzumab target

     

●      Anti CD52

●      CD52 is present on most lymphocytes


What are poor prognostic factors in T-PLL?         

 

·       age > 65 years

·       presence of serous effusions

·       hepatic or CNS involvement

·       bulky lymphadenopathy

·       very high absolute lymphocyte counts

·       complex karyotype

·       very high TCL1A protein

·       bone marrow suppression

·       or organ dysfunction

 

What is a useful IHC stain you can do on the BM to show T-PLL?

 

●      nuclear and cytoplasmic positivity for TCL1 oncoprotein

●      Must first prove you are dealing with a T cell neoplasm (by flow)

●      Because HCL can express too

●      TCL1 overexpression is highly specific for T-PLL within T cell lymphomas

 

 

What is the STAT gene?

 

●      Members of the signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) protein family intracellular transcription factors

●      Mediate many aspects of cellular immunity, proliferation, apoptosis and differentiation.

●      They are primarily activated by membrane receptor-associated Janus kinases (JAK).

●      Dysregulation of this pathway is frequently observed in primary tumors and leads to increased angiogenesis which enhances the survival of tumors and immunosuppression.

Caveats and Pearls

•        Old patient with HSM, skin infiltration

•        Distinctive morphology is best evaluated by peripheral blood smear - blebs

•        The dual CD4+/CD8+ immunophenotype is unique

•        No pan-T antigen loss

•        TCL1 positivity is unique

•        TdT, CD1a negative

•        Inv(14)

*T-LGLL T-cell Large Granular Lymphocytic Leukemia

·       Essential: (1) an increase in circulating cytotoxic T cells (often 2 × 109/L but may be lower); (2) a T-cell population with an aberrant phenotype, usually CD8-positive and with downregulation of CD5 and/or CD7 and/or abnormal expression of CD16 and NK cell–associated receptors; (3) evidence of T-cell monoclonality.

·       Desirable: demonstration of intrasinusoidal cytotoxic lymphocyte infiltrates in the bone marrow by immunohistochemistry; demonstration of STAT3 or STAT5B mutation.

 

What is T-cell Large Granular Lymphocytic Leukemia? (T-LGLL)

       

●      Heterogeneous disorder

●      Characterized by:

○      An increased number of PB LGLs (usually to 2 - 20 x 10E9/L)

■      Note - disagreement about the degree of lymphocytosis, which is not necessary for diagnosis as long as you have increased LGLs

○      Must be persistent (> 6 months)

●      Cytopenias predominate

●      Splenomegaly is common

●      No clearly identified cause

●      EBV negative

 

What type of T cell is T-LGL derived from?

 

●      Cytotoxic/suppressor T cell (CD8+)

3 classic disease associations of T-LGL?

 

●      RA

●      Acquired red cell aplasia → T-LGL is the most likely lymphoid neoplasm associated with acquired RCA -> pure red cell aplasia

●      PNH

 

How common is T-cell Large Granular Lymphocytic Leukemia? (T-LGLL)   

    

●      2-3% of mature small lymphocytic leukemias

Who gets T-LGLL?        

 

●      M:F 1:1

●      No clear age peak

●      Rare <25 years

●      Most cases 45-75

What is the etiology of T-LGLL?

        

●      Not well understood

●      Theory is sustained immune stimulation (as associated with autoimmune disorders)

What pathways are dysregulated in T-LGLL?

                    

●      FASL/FAS[QZ1] 

○      members of the tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-receptor and TNF family

○      Increased levels of FASL in serum leading to neutropenia

●      MAPK, IK3K/AKT, NF-kappaB, JAK/STAT also affected

●      1/3 carry STAT3 mutations

What is unique about the lymphocytes in T-LGLL?   

    

●      Clonal T-cell LGLs → but they retain many phenotypic and functional properties of normal cytotoxic T lymphocyte effector memory cells


What are the areas of involvement in T-LGLL?     

  

●      Blood, Bone marrow

●      Liver, spleen

●      Rarely skin

●      LNopathy rare!!

What is the clinical course of T-LGLL?    

   

●      Indolent → some people feel it’s better classified as a clonal disorder of uncertain significance rather than a leukemia

●      Neutropenia most common

●      Anemia

●      Thrombocytopenia

●      Splenomegaly

●      Association with RA or autoimmune disorder (30%), MDS, PNH, AA, acquired red cell aplasia

●      Othe lymphoid neoplasms - MGUS, SMM, PCM, LPL

●      60% of patients symptomatic at presentation

●      RA/Neutropenia/Splenomegaly may mimic Felty syndrome

 

Typical lymphocyte range in T-LGLL?

●      Lymphocyte count 2-20x10^9/L

What is the diagnostic cutoff for T-LGLs in T-LGLL? 

 

●      Disagreement about level of lymphocytosis

○      >2 x 10^9/L frequently associated with large clonal proliferation

○      Can be <2 x 10^9/L and still have diagnosis

What are other reasons for oligoclonal/clonal expansion of T-LGLs?        

 

●      Many situations for oligoclonal

○      Post-transplant LPD

●      Clonal T-LGLs seen in:

○      Low-grade B-cell malignancies (HCL, CLL)

○      Underlying hematological or non-hematological malignancies (in CD4+ cases)

What are the morphological features of T-LGLL?    

   

 

●      LGLs predominant in blood & BM

●      Morphological features

○      Moderate to abundant cytoplasm

○      Fine or coarse azurophilic granules (contain cytotoxic substances → TIA, granzyme B)

●      Visible from low power

●      Look for other cytopenias → anemia and neutropenia (thrombocytopenia is NOT common)

●      If you are suspicious

○      Flow the PB (LPD flow)

○      Send for T cell clonality

What are the ultrastructural characteristics of LGL granules? 

      

●      Parallel tubular arrays

What are the BM findings in T-LGLL?

       

●      Variable cellularity

○      Normocellular or hypocellular in 50%

○      Hypercellular in 50%

●      AA

●      PRCA

●      Left shifted granulopoiesis

●      Mild/moderate reticulin fibrosis

●      Infiltration pattern

○      Interstitial/intrasinusoidal infiltrates that may be difficult to identify by morphology

○      May be very subtle

●      Frequent non-neoplastic lymphoid aggregates

CD3 immunohistochemical study reveals the characteristic intrasinusoidal / linear infiltrates of T LGLL cells in the bone marrow biopsy; original magnification 400x. The intrasinusoidal / linear arrays of T-LGLL cells in the bone marrow biopsy are positive for CD8; original magnification 400x. Bone marrow intrasinusoidal / linear arrays of T-LGLL expressing granzyme B; original magnification 400x. Bone marrow intrasinusoidal / linear arrays of T-LGLL expressing TIA1; original magnification 400x.

 

What IHC would you order on the biopsy to evaluate for T-LGL?

 

●      IHC → CD20, 3, 4, 8, 57 or 56 (if suspect true NK neoplasm) or EBER (if you suspect aggressive NK cell neoplasm)

●      Image below

○      Note CD8 (membrane stain) highlighting sinusoidal pattern

○      TIA highlights granules and is less intense than CD8 or CD3

 



What is the pattern of splenic involvement in T-LGLL?

       

●      Infiltration and expansion of red pulp cords and sinusoids

●      Sparing of hyperplastic white pulp

What is T-LGLL variant? 

      

●      Cases morphologically resemble T-LGLL → but have NK-cell immunophenotype

○      Negative for sCD3, and TCR

○      These are classified with the NK-cell disorders


Natali Pflug, T-LGLL: variety is the spice of this leukemia, Blood, 2023,

What is the immunophenotype of T-LGLL?    

   

●      Mature cytotoxic/suppressor T-cell phenotype

○      CD3(+), CD8(+) with coexpression of CD16(+) and CD57(+), CD94(+), TCR-α/β(+)

○      CD5/CD7 loss is common

○      CD57 [QZ2] and CD16 [QZ3] in >80% of cases (cytotoxic/suppressor T-cell phenotype; CD57 activation marker)

○      CD56 infrequent (in CAP book: NK markers CD16 CD56 CD94 are frequently detected)

○      CAP book: most specific for T-LGLL vs reactive T-LGL is isolated presence of a distinct and expanded population of CD8dim/CD57+ T-cells, complete or partial loss CD5, expression of CD16

●      IHC:

○      TIA1 (also stains neutrophils), Granzyme B, Granzyme M (cytotoxic/suppressor T-cell phenotype)

●      Uncommon variants:

○      CD4+ A/B TCR = majority cases

○      CD8+ Gamma Delta TCR cases (rare reports)

○      CD4/CD8 negative Gamma delta TCR cases

 



How would you phrase your comment for flow showing increased T-LGLs?

 

●      “Flow cytometry shows an increase in CD8(+), CD57(+) T cells with the immunophenotype of T-LGL. An increase in T-LGLs may be seen in many non-neoplastic disorders (list some egs) and clinical correlation is absolutely essential. TCR clonality studies can be performed if clinically indicated”.

 

Are TCR genes rearranged in T-LGLL?        

 

●      YES

●      Recommend sending for TCR gene rearrangement when working up possible T-LGL

●      TRG gene rearranged in all cases regardless of TCR expression

●      TRB gene rearranged in cases expressing Alpha Beta TCR (but may be germline in gamma delta forms)

What are the genetic abnormalities in T-LGLL?        

 

●      STAT3 mutations in 1/3rd (40%) of cases

○      Affect SH2 domain of STAT

○      Gain of function

○      Also in L-HES, CLPD-NK

●      STAT5B mutations → associated with more aggressive disease

○      Also in T-PLL, HSTCL

●      No karyotypic abnormalities

 

Why are T-LGLs resistant to apoptosis?

 

●      Defective FAS (CD95)

●      Have high levels of FAS ligand in sera

●      This elevation is purported to be important in the pathogenesis of neutropenia

What is the prognosis of T-LGLL? 

      

●      Good → indolent and non-progressive disease

●      Stable for many years; spontaneous remissions are possible

●      Some people feel it’s better classified as a clonal disorder of uncertain significance rather than a leukemia

●      Median survival 161 months

●      No difference in survival with or without STAT3 mutation

●      STAT5B mutations associated with → more aggressive disease

●      Note associations with RA & PRCA & ALPS

What causes the most morbidity in T-LGLL?     

  

●      Cytopenias

●      Especially neutropenia

Does T-LGLL transform?

       

●      RARELY transform into peripheral T-cell Lymphoma

Can T-LGLL spontaneously remit?        

 

●      Yes, cases have been reported

What are treatment modalities for T-LGLL? 

      

●      Cyclosporine, low dose Methotrexate = first line

●      Cyclophosphamide, corticosteroids

●      Methotrexate preferred if RA

●      Splenectomy, but no correction of cytopenia

 

What autoimmune condition may mimic T-LGLL → classic DDx?

 

●      RA with Felty syndrome = RA, neutropenia, splenomegaly triad

●      Differ from T-LGLL with clonality studies - 30% of T-LGLL patients have RA

●      Age of onset of both Felty syndrome and T-LGLL is about 15 years after RA diagnosis

 

Caveats and Pearls

•        Mid-age to old

•        6 months and more than 2x109/l LGL

•        Interstitial or intersinusoidal

•        CD3+CD8+CD16+CD57+CD45RA+ ab T

•        STAT3, STAT5B

•        FAS/FASL apoptosis pathway dysregulation

•        RA/PRCA/ALPS association

* CLPD-NKs Chronic Lymphoproliferative Disorder of NK Cells

 

What are Chronic lymphoproliferative disorders of NK cells (CLPD-NKs)?

       

●      NK-LGLL in new WHO: a neoplasm characterized by a persistent increase in peripheral blood NK cells (usually > 2 × 109/L) and a chronic indolent clinical course

●      Rare and heterogenous disorders

●      >6 months of increased NK-cell count in blood (usually >2 x 10^9)

●      No cause identified

●      Hard to distinguish between this and reactive causes

●      EBV negative

 

What causes Chronic lymphoproliferative disorders of NK cells (CLPD-NKs)?    

   

●      Unknown

●      Postulated theory is stimulation of innate immunity due to viral infection

●      1/3rd of cases have STAT3 activating mutation affecting the SH2 domain (just like T-LGLL)

 

What drug may produce a sustained increase in NK cells that may be monoclonal?

 

●      Dasatanib → can produce a sustained increase in NK cells that may be monoclonal

●      May also be encountered in many conditions such as → autoimmune or viral infections

What are the clinical features of Chronic lymphoproliferative disorders of NK cells (CLPD-NKs)?        

 

●      Asymptomatic

●      Cytopenias (anemia and neutropenia)

●      LAD and organomegaly are uncommon

Can Chronic lymphoproliferative disorders of NK cells (CLPD-NKs) be associated with other medical conditions - give 4 eg.s?     

 

●      Yes

●      Autoimmune disorder

●      Solid tumours

●      Hematological neoplasms

●      Neuropathy


What do circulating cells look like in Chronic lymphoproliferative disorders of NK cells (CLPD-NKs)?    

   

●      Intermediate size

●      Round nuclei

●      Mature condensed chromatin

●      Moderate basophilic cytoplasm

●      Fine or coarse azurophilic granules

What is the pattern of BM involvement with Chronic lymphoproliferative disorders of
NK cells (CLPD-NKs)?       

 

●      IHC can show the Intrasinusoidal infiltration in the bone marrow and spleen

●      same as T LGL


What is the immunophenotype of Chronic lymphoproliferative disorders of NK cells (CLPD-NKs)?        

 

●      sCD3 negative

●      cCD3 epsilon positive

●      CD16 positive

●      weak CD56+

●      Diminished expression of CD2, CD7, CD57 possible

●      Abnormal uniform expression for CD8 is reported

●      Abnormal expression of KIR (killer cell Ig receptor) in all cases either complete lack or restricted isoform expression

●      Bright CD94/NKG2A → lectin expressed on NK cells that recognizes MHC class I

●      Positive cytotoxic markers (TIA1, granzyme B, Granzyme M)

 

What are the genetic changes in Chronic lymphoproliferative disorders of NK cells (CLPD-NKs)?       

 

●      30% have STAT3 SH2 domain changes

●      25-30% TET2

●      Absence of TR rearrangement → unlike T LGL because not T cells

What is the prognosis of Chronic lymphoproliferative disorders of NK cells (CLPD-NKs)?

        

●      Indolent course

●      No therapy needed

●      In general, management is similar to T-cell LGL leukemia

●      Cytopenias and recurrent infections may occur

●      Some cases have complete remission, or transformation to aggressive NK-disorder

*ATLL Adult T-cell Leukemia/Lymphoma, HTLV-1+

●      Essential: neoplastic lymphoid cell proliferation with mature T-cell phenotype; proven HTLV-1 carriership.

●       Desirable: lymphoid cells with prominent convolutions and lobulation; identification of monoclonal integration of HTLV-1.

 

Q. 5 types of Nodal T-cell Lymphomas?

 

●      ATLL, HTLV-1+

●      ALK+ ALCL

●      ALK- ALCL

●      AITL

●      PTCL, NOS

Q. ATLL Definition?

 

●      Mature peripheral T-cell leukemia/lymphoma caused by human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) infection

●      Derived from helper T cell


Q. Viral cause of ATLL

 

●      Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1)

 

Q. 4 clinical ATLL variants?           

 

●      Acute (leukemic) → most aggressive subtype

●      Lymphomatous

●      Chronic

●      Smoldering

●      5th clinical variant has been proposed: Cutaneous

●      CLASS

Q. What are non-neoplastic diseases associated with HTLV-1?

 

●      HTLV-1-associated myelopathy (tropical spastic paraparesis)

●      HTLV-1-associated infective dermatitis

●      Other HTLV-1 inflammatory disorders

○      Uveitis

○      Thyroiditis

○      Pneumonitis

○      Myositis

 

T-DUMP (on a squatty potty)

 

Q. What is the frequency of ATLL among carriers of HTLV1?

 

●      2.5%

 

Q. Area spared of LAD in ATLL?

 

●      Mediastinum

Q. 2 clinical findings o/e with ATLL?

 

●      Hepatosplenomegaly, skin lesions

 

Q. 3 typical investigation findings (2 lab & 1 imaging) with ATLL?

●      Leukemic involvement

●      hypercalcemia

●      lytic lesions

●      Hepatosplenomegaly

 

Q. What are the non-malignant bone marrow features of ATLL?

 

●      Prominent osteoclastic activity

 


Q. Name 1 novel targeted therapy for ATLL

 

●      Mogamulizumab (anti-CCR4) -> indicated in ATLL, CTCL, PTCL


Q. Median survival: for acute and lymphomatous variants of ATLL?

 

●      6-12 months


Q. Surrogate marker for HTLV-1 integration into ATLL

 

●      Seropositivity for HTLV-1

○      Useful in areas with low prevalence of HTLV-1 infection


Q. ATLL: Low power pattern of LN infiltration?

 

●      *Diffuse effacement* of LN architecture

 




Q. Description for ATLL cells in PB?

 

●      "Flower cells"

 

 


Q. Unique histological feature to look for in bone & BM involved by ATLL?

 

●      Osteoclast activation and bone resorption


Q. ATLL Immunophenotype?

 

●      Pan-T-cell antigens (+)

○      CD2, CD3, CD5, and T-cell receptor (TCR)-α/β

○      90% of cases are CD4(+), CD8(-)

■      Rare cases can be CD4(-), CD8(+), or CD4(+), CD8(+)

○      CD25(+), CCR4(+), HLA-DR(+), CD62 (L-selectin) (+)

●      FOXP3(+), which is marker of regulatory T cells

●      Ki67 high proliferation index

●      IRF-4/MUM1(+/-), CD15(-/+), *CD30(-/+)*, CD56(-/+)

 

Neg for PD1, CD7, TdT, TCL1, ALK, B-cell antigens, Myeloid antigens, Cytotoxic markers

Is ATLL CD4 or CD8 pos?

 

●      Most cases CD4(+), CD8(-)

Q. ATLL: complex or simple CGs?

 

●      Complex cytogenetic abnormalities


Q. ATLL: What has been integrated into host genome?       

 

●      Monoclonal integration of HTLV-1 into host genome

 

Q. What is the mutation in ATLL?

●      25% of ATLL cases have CCR4


Q. ATLL Top DDx?

 

●      T-PLL: (Usually CD4(+) or exhibit CD4(+)/CD8(+) coexpression)

●      PTCL, NOS: leukemic involvement

●      AITL

●      ALCL

●      MF/SS (Usually CD4(+) or exhibit CD4(+)/CD8(+) coexpression)

Classic cytologic finding of ATLL?

 

●      Multilobulated nucleus, "flower cell"

Classic cytologic findings of PTCL, NOS?

 

●      Irregular, monomorphic or pleomorphic cells

Classic cytologic findings of AITL?

 

●      Small to irregular cells with clear cytoplasm

Classic cytologic findings of ALCL?

 

●      Horseshoe- or kidney-shaped large nuclei → “Hallmark cells”

Classic cytologic findings of MF/SS?

 

●      Cerebriform cell

 

Caveats and Pearls

•        Flower cells are best observed on peripheral blood smear

•        4 variants, HTLV1, CD4+, T-reg, FOXP3+, CCXR4, Mogamulizumab

*Aggressive NK-cell Leukemia

·       Essential: presentation with fever, constitutional symptoms, and a leukaemic blood picture; systemic (multiorgan) involvement by neoplastic lymphoid cells with an NK-cell immunophenotype; absence of T-cell receptor protein expression and/or clonal TR rearrangement.

·       Desirable: EBER positivity (positive in ~90% of cases); haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

 

What is Aggressive NK-cell leukemia?

        

•        Systemic neoplastic proliferation of NK cells with aggressive clinical course

•        EBV positive

Who gets Aggressive NK-cell leukemia? 

 

●      Asians

●      Middle age (median age 40)

●      Two incidence peaks - 3rd and 5th decades of life

●      M=F

What causes Aggressive NK-cell leukemia?     

   

●      Unknown

●      EBV-associated

●      Might represent leukemic counterpart of extranodal NK/T cell lymphoma - nasal type

What tissues are involved in Aggressive NK-cell leukemia?    

 

●      Blood, Bone Marrow, Liver, Spleen

●      Any organ can be (ie overlap with extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma)

What disease can Aggressive NK-cell leukemia overlap with and why?     

   

●      Extranodal involvement in Aggressive NK-cell leukemia can overlap with NK/T-cell lymphoma


How do patients with Aggressive NK-cell leukemia present?     

   

●      Fever, constitutional symptoms, leukemia blood picture

●      Circulating leukemic cells low or high (a few percent to >80% of the leukocytes)

●      LDH increased

●      HSmegaly common

●      LAD

●      Effusions common

●      May develop coagulopathy and HLH


What is the morphology of Aggressive NK-cell leukemia?         

 

●      Range of appearances

●      Cells look like LGLs, slightly larger

●      Atypical nuclei featuring enlargement, irregular folding, open chromatin or distinct nucleoli

●      Ample pale or slightly basophilic cytoplasm

●      Coarse or fine azurophilic granules


What are the BM findings in Aggressive NK-cell leukemia?         

 

●      Massive diffuse, focal, or subtle infiltration

●      Reactive histiocytes with hemophagocytosis common

●      Necrosis and apoptotic bodies are common

                                                     
What is the immunophenotype of Aggressive NK-cell leukemia?     

  

●      CD2+, cCD3-epsilon+, CD56+, CD16+ (>75%), EBER

●      sCD3-, CD5-, CD57-, CD8-

●      Positive for cytotoxic molecules (TIA, Gran B) and EBER

●      Note: identical to NK/T cell lymphoma, except CD16 is positive in >75% and CD8-

●      Loss of CD2, CD7, CD5 are common

●      Note: elevated FASL in serum


What is the genetic profile of Aggressive NK-cell leukemia?  

 

●      No recurrent cytogenetic abnormalities (ExpertPath)


Is Aggressive NK-cell leukemia EBV positive or negative  

      

●      Positive in 85-100%


What is the prognosis of Aggressive NK-cell leukemia?         

 

●      Median survival < 2 months

●      Hemophagocytic syndrome

●      Coagulopathy & multiorgan failure contribute to morbidity & mortality

 

Caveats and Pearls

• CD16 and CD56 are expressed by NK-cells, whereas CD57 is expressed by T-LGL

*SS Sezary Syndrome

 

Sézary syndrome (SS) is defined by triad of?    

 

  1. Pruritic erythroderma
  2. Presence of clonally related neoplastic T-cells with cerebriform nuclei (Sézary cells) in the skin, lymph nodes, and peripheral blood
  3. Generalized lymphadenopathy

 

●      By definition you must have → blood & cutaneous involvement

●      Lymphoma cells in skin, blood, and lymph node are all clonally related

 


Name ONE additional criterion that is required for the diagnosis → at least 1 of what 3 things?    

 

●      Absolute Sézary cell count ≥ 1000/uL(1.0x109/L) or

●      Increased CD4:CD8 ratio > 10 or

●      T-cell immunophenotypic aberrancies demonstrated by flow cytometric immunophenotyping (loss of CD7 and CD26 is characteristic)

●      Note: all normal people will have low numbers of C4(+) helper T cells with loss of CD7

Loss of what T cell marker is characteristic for SS?   

 

●      CD7

●      CD26

 

Can SS present de novo?    

 

●      Yes

●      SS presents de novo in most patients


SS may be preceded by what other disease? 

 

●      Can be preceded by mycosis fungoides (MF)

●      Cases should be designated as "SS preceded by MF"

●      Presents de novo in most patients

Skin changes in SS? 

 

●      Intractable pruritus and generalized erythroderma with edema (≥ 80% of skin surface)

●      May have pruritus without erythema/rash

●      May be similar to Mycosis fungoides

●      Biopsy may or may not show epidermotropism

 


Extracutaneous sites of involvement in SS?

  

●      Lymph nodes, lung, liver, spleen

●      Central nervous system, other organs

●      Bone marrow (BM) → relatively spared


SS treatment options?

         

●      Most treatments are palliative, not curative

●      Total skin electron beam radiation with nonmyeloablative allogeneic SCT may be curative

 

SS prognosis?  

  

●      Poor survival: Median < 2.5 years

●      SS PB findings

●      Threshold # for Dx?

 

What features must be confirmed for diagnosis? How do you confirm them?

    

●      Sézary cells (cells with cerebriform nuclei) → must be >1 x 10^9/L (> 1,000/µL) with:

○      Confirmed T-cell clonality or

○      Increased CD4:CD8 ratio > 10 or

○      T-cell immunophenotypic aberrancies demonstrated by flow cytometric immunophenotyping

Skin changes in SS are very similar to what other disease?

   

●      Mycosis fungoides (image)

 


In SS lymph nodes show?

 

●      Partial or total effacement of normal architecture


Classic descriptor for Sézary cells in PB?  

 

●      Cells with cerebriform nuclei (Sézary cells)

●      May lack the characteristic brain-like appearance and just look like an oddball lymphocyte

●      Mature chromatin

●      Nuclear irregularities

●      May be much larger than normal mature lymphs

●      Morphology is unreliable → IP necessary for Dx

 

 

●      Image: large Sezary cell with cerebriform nuclei

 

 

●      Image: small normal lymph and neutrophil (top left) for comparison with 5 Sezary cells

 

 

●      Image: less typical Sezary cell (not classic cerebriform)

 

 

●      Image: normal lymph, Sezary cell & monocyte


Sézary cells are not completely specific - in what other scenarios may they be seen?

     

●      Especially small forms can be seen in reactive conditions

●      Most large cells are neoplastic

Is Sézary syndrome (SS) a CD4 or CD8 pos T cell lymphoma?

 

●      CD4(+), CD8(-)

●      Derived from a helper T cell

Sézary syndrome (SS) immunophenotype?

  

●      Pan-T-cell antigens (+), TCR-αβ(+) by IHC or flow cytometry

●      CD4(+), CD8(-)

●      CD3 and CD5(+)

●      Loss or dim expression of ≥ 1 T-cell antigens (frequently CD7)

●      CD25(-)

●      CD26(-)

●      TRBC1 clonality

  [QZ4] 

 

●      ALC = absolute lymphocyte count

●      CD3 & CD4(+)

●      Aberrant loss of CD7 and CD26 (present on normal lymphs in green)

●      Note: all normal people will have low numbers of C4(+) helper T cells with loss of CD7

●      May report as % of CD4(+), CD7 & CD26(-) of all T cells

Sézary syndrome (SS) Top Differential Diagnoses (5)

  

●      Nonneoplastic causes of erythroderma

○      Drug reaction → may cause eosinophilia and lymphocytosis too. Generally acute onset and temporally related to drug administration

●      CD4+ Helper T-cell neoplasm involving blood: T-PLL, rare ALCL, PTCL-NOS, ATLL

●      Leukemia cutis (especially monocytic leukemia)

●      MF with leukemic involvement

●      Reactive lymphocytosis

 

Overlap Between Sézary Syndrome and Mycosis Fungoides

·       Rare case of SS preceded by classic MF: Diagnose as "SS preceded by MF"

·       MF patient without erythroderma may have blood involvement: Diagnose as "MF with leukemic involvement"

 

Caveats and Pearls

·       Flow cytometric analysis should meet one of the following criteria:

·       Sezary cell count >1000/μL

·       CD4:CD8 ratio greater than 10

·       Abnormal CD4+ T-cell population that shows loss of CD7 or CD26

Primary cutaneous T NK lymphomas

MF Mycosis Fungoides

 

What is Mycosis Fungoides?   

 

●      Primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma characterized by:

○      Epidermotropism

○      Clinical course showing stepwise evolution of → patches, plaques, and tumors

●      Derived from a CD4+ helper T cell

 

MF stage?

 

          

●      Early stage with patches

MF stage?          

 

 

●      Disseminated plaque stage.
          

MF stage?

 

 

●      MF tumour stage


Does MF have an aggressive or indolent clinical course? 

   

●      Overall indolent clinical course


What is the most important predictor of prognosis in MF?

 

●      Clinical stage


What process is thought to contribute to MF pathogenesis

 

●      Chronic antigenic stimulation

What is the issue with skin biopsies from premycotic and some early patch stage lesions?       

 

●      Often nondiagnostic


Macroscopic description of MF Patch stage:

     

●      Circumscribed lesions with discoloration


Macroscopic description of MF Plaque stage:  

 

  • Elevated, palpable lesions

Macroscopic description of MF Tumor stage:

 

  • Combination of patches, plaques, and ulcerated tumors exophytic, ulceration common

 

MF histo findings in patch and thin plaque stage

      

●      Superficial band-like or lichenoid infiltrate [QZ5] of dermis, may begin to infiltrate basal layer or epidermis in early patch stage


MF histo findings in thick plaque stage     

 

●      Dense, subepidermal band-like infiltrate

●      Many cerebriform lymphs

●      Prominent epidermotropism and Pautrier microabscesses

MF histo findings in tumor stage     

   

●      Prominent dermal infiltrate

MF stage?     

 

 

●      MF tumour stage with histological transformation to a large cell lymphoma (may be CD30+)

Early or late stage MF?     

 

    

 

●      Early MF with infiltrates of atypical, haloed lymphocytes in the basal layer of epidermis.

MF stage?     

 

 

●      Plaque lesion of MF with a dense, epidermotropic infiltrate of atypical, cerebriform lymphocytes and characteristic Pautrier micro abscesses.


Large cell transformation of MF is said to occur when large tumor cells are > ____% 

      

●      Large tumor cells are > 25%

                                                
What is Epidermotropism?    

 

 

●      Lymphocytosis of epidermis without spongiosis [Spongiosis is mainly inter-cellular edema in the epidermis]


Criteria for "large cell transformation" 

 

●      Large tumor cells are > 25%

●      May be CD30+

Name 4 MF variants 

 

●      Folliculotropic

●      Syringotropic

●      Granulomatous slack skin

●      Pagetoid reticulosis

 

Subtype

Classic Alibert-Bazin MF

Folliculotropic MF

Pagetoid Reticulosis

Granulomatous Slack Skin

Clinical Features

Patches → plaques → tumors; common on sun-protected areas; may progress to erythroderma.

Hair follicle involvement; advanced: head/neck tumors, poor prognosis; early: patches, favorable prognosis.

Psoriasiform or hyperkeratotic lesions on extremities.

Papules/plaques in folds → skin laxity.

Histopathology

Atypical T-cells; epidermotropism.

Neoplastic follicular infiltrates; may show follicular mucinosis.

Pagetoid proliferation of atypical T-cells.

Granulomas, elastophagocytosis, atypical T-cells.

Prognosis

Indolent; rare extracutaneous spread worsens prognosis.

Variable; immune privilege disruption in hair follicles.

Indolent; often localized.

Indolent; increased risk of secondary malignancies.

MF Immunophenotype?

 

●      It is a cutaneous CD4(+) T cell lymphoma, derived from helper T cell

●      CD2(+), CD3(+), CD5(+), TCR-αβ/βF1(+)

●      CD4(+), CD8(-)

●      CD7(-), CD26(-)

●      CD30 usually expressed by large cells

●      CD45/LCA(+), CLA(+), CD52(+), CD25(-/+)

●      Ig(-), B cell markers (-)

What are the characteristics of Pagetoid reticulosis?    

  

 

●      The presence of patches or plaques with an intraepidermal proliferation of neoplastic T-cells


MF Top Differential Diagnoses?     

 

●      Drug reaction, inflammatory dermatoses

●      Sézary syndrome → MF can develop blood involvement with disease progression (leukemic involvement)

●      Primary cutaneous CD30(+) T-cell LPD

●      Primary cutaneous γ/δ T-cell lymphoma

●      Rare variants of T-cell lymphoma involving skin

What is this cell?

 

 

●      Sezary cell in PB

 

Caveats and Pearls

·       Overlapping features with SS – more a dermpath thing

·      3 stages and 4 variants

Primary cutaneous CD30+ T-cell LPDs - Lymphomatoid Papulosis (LyP)



The category “Primary cutaneous CD30(+) T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder” encompasses what 2 entities?

         

●      Lymphomatoid Papulosis (LyP)

●      Cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma (C-ALCL)

 

What is Lymphomatoid Papulosis (LyP)?

 

●      Chronic, self-healing and recurrent erythematous papules/nodules on skin of trunk and extremities

●      Composed of large, atypical cells in marked inflammatory background

●      *"Primary cutaneous CD30(+) T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder"*

Gross description of dermatologic lesions in LyP?

   

●      Chronic, self-healing and recurrent erythematous papules/nodules on skin of trunk and extremities

●      The erythematous papule evolves into a red-brown, often hemorrhagic, papulovesicular or papulopustular lesion over days to weeks

 

Lymphomatoid Papulosis prognosis?

 

●      Usually remains confined to skin

●      Excellent prognosis

●      Waxing and waning clinical course; can persist for decades

●      Individual skin lesions spontaneously regress within 3-12 weeks

●      10-year disease-specific survival of ∼ 100%

Subset of LYP cases arise in patients with what other 2 diseases?

 

●      Mycosis fungoides (MF)

●      Cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma (C-ALCL)


How many histologic subtypes of Lymphomatoid Papulosis are there?

 

●      6 histologic types represent a spectrum of disease

●      Types A, B, C, D, E & F

Lymphomatoid Papulosis Most common histologic type

 

●      Type A

Lymphomatoid Papulosis Least common histologic type

 

●      Type B


Describe type A Lymphomatoid Papulosis?   

 

●      Most common

●      Scattered large atypical Reed-Sternberg-like cells

 

 

●      Numerous inflammatory cells including small lymphocytes, histiocytes, granulocytes


Describe type B Lymphomatoid Papulosis? 

 

●      Uncommon (< 10%)

●      Mimics MF with epidermotropism and band-like dermal infiltrate

●      Lymphoid cells with cerebriform nuclei

Describe type C Lymphomatoid Papulosis? 

 

●      Clusters or sheets of large atypical lymphoid cells with relatively few admixed inflammatory cells

Describe type D Lymphomatoid Papulosis?

 

●      Marked epidermotropism; CD8(+)

●      Gamma Delta

Describe type type E Lymphomatoid Papulosis?

 

●      Angioinvasive with necrotic surface

●      CD8 (+)

Describe type F Lymphomatoid Papulosis? 

 

●      Folliculotropic or syringotropic


The large atypical cells in Lymphomatoid Papulosis are usually CD____ pos?

 

●      *CD30(+)*

●      Large, atypical cells are CD30(+), ALK(-), usually CD4(+)

●      Type D: Atypical lymphocytes express CD8

LYP immunophenotype. 1) Large, atypical cells? 2) Small lymphocytes?

 

●      Large, atypical cells are CD30(+), ALK(-), usually CD4(+)

●      Type D: Atypical lymphocytes express CD8

●      Small lymphocytes are T cells: Usually CD7(-)

How common are T-cell receptor rearrangements in LyP?

 

●      Monoclonal T-cell receptor rearrangements in ∼ 60%


Rearrangements of what 2 genes may rarely be seen in LYP?

 

●      DUSP22-IRF4 (uncommon)

●      NPM1-TYK2 (5%)

 

What are the characteristics of LyP with 6p rearrangement?

 

●      Rearrangement of DUSP22-IRF4

●      Resembles transformed MF (tumor stage MF)

●      Extensive epidermotropism

●      CD8+ or double negative


What type lymphocyte (B vs T) are the small cells seen in Lymphomatoid Papulosis infiltrate  

 

●      Small lymphocytes are T cells: Usually CD7(-)



Lymphomatoid Papulosis Top Differential Diagnoses?

 

●      Primary cutaneous ALCL

●      Systemic ALCL with cutaneous involvement

●      Classical Hodgkin lymphoma

●      MF with transformation

In many cases, LyP cannot be distinguished from what other disease without clinical information/follow-up

 

●      Cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma (C-ALCL)

 

 

Primary cutaneous CD30+ T-cell LPDs - Primary cutaneous ALCL

 

What is Primary Cutaneous Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (C-ALCL)?

 

●      Cutaneous lymphoma composed of large T cells that express CD30 (> 75%)

What 2 entities are included under umbrella term CD30(+) T-cell lymphoproliferative disorders

 

●      C-ALCL

●      Lymphomatoid papulosis (LyP)


C-ALCL common sites of involvement?  

 

●      Face, trunk, and extremities

Gross description of typical C-ALCL skin lesion?  

 

●      Solitary nodule or localized nodules/papules; ± ulceration

●      Presents with multiple nodules or multifocal in ∼ 20%

C-ALCL Extracutaneous dissemination in ~ ____ % of patients

 

●      10%

C-ALCL prognosis?

 

●      Spontaneous regression can occur; relapse is common

●      Favorable prognosis with 10-year survival of ~ 90%

C-ALCL typical histologic findings?

 

●      Diffuse infiltrates of large neoplastic cells mainly located in dermis; can extend into subcutaneous tissue

●      Variable inflammatory cell infiltrate in background

●      Anaplastic cells in most cases; ~ 20% non-anaplastic

C-ALCL: What % of neoplastic large cells are CD30(+)?

 

●      > 75% of neoplastic large cells CD30(+) as per diagnostic criteria

What aberrant T cell markers are expressed by C-ALCL?

 

●      Cytotoxic markers on a CD4+ helper T cell population

●      CD4(+), cytotoxic proteins(+), cutaneous lymphocyte antigen (CLA) (+/-), CD56(-/+), EMA(-), CD15(-), ALK(-)

C-ALCL immunophenotype?

 

●      CD4(+), cytotoxic proteins(+), cutaneous lymphocyte antigen (CLA) (+/-), CD30+

●      CD56(-/+), EMA(-), CD15(-), ALK(-), CTL+, MUM1+

Specific cytogenetic marker associated with C-ALCL?  

 

●      No specific cytogenetic abnormalities identified
Monoclonal T-cell receptor rearrangements

C-ALCL shows rearrangements of what 2 genes?

 

●      Monoclonal T-cell receptor gene rearrangements

●      Rearrangements of:

○      DUSP22-IRF4 locus on 6p25.3 in ∼ 20%

○      NPM1-TYK2 in ∼ 5%


C-ALCL Top Differential Diagnoses?

    

●      Systemic ALK(-) ALCL with cutaneous involvement

●      Large cell transformation of mycosis fungoides

●      Lymphomatoid papulosis, type C

●      Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, NOS

 

Subcutaneous Panniculitis-Like T-cell lymphoma

 

What is Subcutaneous Panniculitis-Like T-Cell Lymphoma (SPTCL)

   

●      Cytotoxic and T-cell receptor (TCR)-αβ(+) T-cell lymphoma that preferentially involves subcutaneous tissue

 

Subcutaneous Panniculitis-Like T-Cell Lymphoma is a lymphoma of what T cell type?

    

●      Cytotoxic and T-cell receptor (TCR)-αβ(+) T-cells

TCR-γδ(+) neoplasms are now classified as?

 

●      *Primary cutaneous γδ T-cell lymphoma*

●      Definition of subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma (SPTCL) substantially revised in WHO 2008 classification; no change in WHO 2016

●      TCR-γδ(+) neoplasms are now classified as primary cutaneous γδ T-cell lymphoma

SPTCL clinical presentation? 

 

●      Patients present with solitary or multiple subcutaneous nodules or plaques

●      Legs > arms > trunk

●      Hemophagocytic syndrome in ∼ 15-20% of patients

T or F → SPTCL is clinically aggressive

  

●      F → SPTCL is clinically indolent


What syndrome may be associated with SPTCL  

 

●      Hemophagocytic syndrome in ∼ 15-20% of patients

●      EBV negative

Rx for SPTCL 

 

●      SPTCL is clinically indolent

●      Recent trend toward using single immunosuppressive agents, at least initially

●      Multiagent chemotherapy reserved for patients with progressive disease

SPTCL involves primarily what tissue  

 

●      SPTCL involves primarily *subcutaneous adipose tissue*

●      Involves adipose tissue lobules and spares septa

●      Minimal or no (deep) dermal involvement

●      Lymphoma cells small to intermediate in size


SPTCL microscopic features      

 

●      Involves primarily subcutaneous adipose tissue

●      Involves adipose tissue lobules and spares septa

●      Minimal or no (deep) dermal involvement

●      Lymphoma cells small to intermediate in size

●      Neoplastic cells often rim and disrupt individual adipocyte membrane → lace like pattern of rimming of fat by neoplastic cells eg with CD8 IHC

●      Apoptotic cells, karyorrhectic debris, fat necrosis

●      Infiltrate commonly associated with CD4(+) cells and histiocytes

 



SPTCL immunophenotype 

      

●      βF1/TCR-αβ(+)

●      Pan-T-cell antigens (+)

●      CD8(+), CD4(-)

●      Cytotoxic proteins (+)

●      Monoclonal TCR gene rearrangements

SPTCL top DDx  

 

●      Lupus erythematosus panniculitis

●      Primary cutaneous γδ T-cell lymphoma[QZ6] 

●      Atypical lymphocytic lobular panniculitis

●      Primary cutaneous CD30(+) lymphoproliferative disorders eg ALCL

 

 

Primary cutaneous T-Cell Lymphomas, Rare subtypes

 

What is Primary Cutaneous γ/δ T-Cell Lymphoma

 

●      Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma that expresses γ/δ T-cell receptor

Clinical presentation of Primary Cutaneous γ/δ T-Cell Lymphoma 

 

●      Patients present with skin lesions; often multiple

○      Epidermal disease can appear as patches or plaques

○      Dermal or subcutaneous disease appears as nodules

●      B-type symptoms are common

●      Lymphoma can spread to other extranodal sites

●      Lymph nodes and bone marrow are rarely involved

●      Hemophagocytic syndrome in subset of patients


What severe condition may be seen in a subset of patients with Primary Cutaneous γ/δ T-Cell Lymphoma 

 

●      Hemophagocytic syndrome in subset of patients

Primary Cutaneous γ/δ T-Cell Lymphoma prognosis

 

●      Poor prognosis despite multiagent chemotherapy ± irradiation

●      Median overall survival: ∼ 15 months

Primary Cutaneous γ/δ T-Cell Lymphoma 3 histologic patterns that are not mutually exclusive 

 

●      Epidermal with minimal or marked epidermotropism

●      Dermal involvement

●      Subcutaneous tissue


Primary Cutaneous γ/δ T-Cell Lymphoma microscopic features

 

●      3 histologic patterns that are not mutually exclusive

○      Epidermal with minimal or marked epidermotropism

○      Dermal involvement

○      Subcutaneous tissue

●      Neoplastic cells often rim adipocytes

○      Often associated with dermal disease

○      Lymphoma cells show spectrum of cell sizes with atypia

○      Apoptosis and necrosis are common


Primary Cutaneous γ/δ T-Cell Lymphoma immunophenotype?

 

●      TCR-δ(+), TCR-γ(+), βF1/TCR-αβ(-)

●      CD2(+), CD3(+), cytotoxic proteins (+), CD56(+)

●      CD4(-), CD8(-) in most cases; CD5(-)

●      Monoclonal rearrangements of TRG and TRD genes

●      ± monoclonal rearrangements of TRB gene

Primary Cutaneous γ/δ T-Cell Lymphoma top DDx

 

●      Benign causes of panniculitis

●      Subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma

●      Primary cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma

●      Pagetoid reticulosis

●      Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified


What is panniculitis 

 

●      Inflammation of subcutaneous adipose tissue

 

Intestinal T-cell and NK-cell lymphoid proliferations and lymphomas

EATL Enteropathy Associated T-Cell Lymphoma

 

What is EATL?   

 

●      Lymphoma arising from intraepithelial T cells of intestine

EATL is usually associated with what underlying disease?

        

●      Celiac disease

What is the Etiology/Pathogenesis of EATL?

   

●      Classical cases of EATL arise in patients with evidence of celiac disease

●      Associated with gluten intolerance

●      Refractory celiac disease is precursor lesion

●      Greatest frequency in areas with high prevalence of celiac disease

●      Association with HLA-DQ2.2, HLA-DQ5, or HLA-DQ8

●      Antibodies to gliadin and tissue transglutaminase

3 HLA types associated with EATL?     

   

●      HLA-DQ2.2, HLA-DQ5, or HLA-DQ8


EATL comprises what % of intestinal T-cell lymphoma with malabsorption     

 

●      ∼ 80-90%

Do most patients EATL have child-onset or adult-onset celiac disease     

 

●        Adult-onset celiac disease

EATL most commonly arises in what part of intestine?

        

●      Jejunum; less frequently in ileum and then duodenum

What clinically dramatic presentation may occur with EATL

        

●      Acute abdo, SBO or perforation

●      Subset of patients present with small bowel obstruction or perforation

●      EATL often initially diagnosed by intestinal resection at time of acute abdomen

EATL prognosis?         

 

●      Prognosis is very poor due to late diagnosis

CT abdo findings with EATL?         

 

●      Enlarged lymph nodes in mesenteric region are common

EATL microscopic findings?   

     

●      Lymph node commonly with partial involvement, paracortical or sinusoidal

●      GI

○      Multiple ulcerating raised mucosal masses seen grossly

○      Transmural infiltration of intestine

●      Lymphoma cells admixed with reactive lymphocytes, histiocytes, or eosinophils

 


EATL immunophenotype?   

 

●      CD3+, CD4-, CD8- (DNT), CD7+, CD5-, CD56-, CD103+, CD30+/-, cytotoxic+

●      CD30 focally (+) in subset of cases

●      TCR: Alpha Beta > Gamma Delta

●      CD8 and CD56 may be positive in a subset

●      CD103 is positive (intestinal T cell marker)


Amplification of chromosome ___q34 may be seen in 58-70% cases of EATL     

 

●       Amplification of 9q34 (58-70% cases)

●      9q34 (58-70% cases)


EATL top DDx       

 

●      Monomorphic epitheliotropic intestinal T-cell lymphoma (MEITL)

●      Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified

●      Extranodal NK-/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type → commonly involves GI tract and must be considered in the DDx

●      Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma

MEITL Monomorphic Epitheliotropic Intestinal T-Cell Lymphoma

 

What is Monomorphic Epitheliotropic Intestinal T-Cell Lymphoma (MEITL)

           

●      T-cell lymphoma arising from intestinal intraepithelial T cells

●      Monomorphic lymphoma cells

Monomorphic Epitheliotropic Intestinal T-Cell Lymphoma arises from what cells?          

 

●      T-cell lymphoma arising from → intestinal intraepithelial T cells

Monomorphic Epitheliotropic Intestinal T-Cell Lymphoma common immunophenotype?

           

●      CD56(+), CD8(+/-), TCRγδ(+), TIA-1 Granzyme

●      CD4-, CD30-, CD103 -/+

Key immunophenotype differences from EATL → MEITL is CD56(+), CD8(+/-), TCRγδ(+)

Monomorphic Epitheliotropic Intestinal T-Cell Lymphoma was formerly designated as

           

●      Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma type 2

Is celiac disease a feature of Monomorphic Epitheliotropic Intestinal T-Cell Lymphoma           

 

●      No

●      No predisposing conditions

Monomorphic Epitheliotropic Intestinal T-Cell Lymphoma most commonly involves what

part of GI tract          

 

●      Jejunum or ileum

What dramatic clinical presentation may patients with Monomorphic Epitheliotropic Intestinal T-Cell Lymphoma have  

 

●      Subset of patients presents with *small bowel obstruction or perforation*

Prognosis for patients with Monomorphic Epitheliotropic Intestinal T-Cell Lymphoma who present with small bowel obstruction or perforation?

 

●      Prognosis poor due to late diagnosis

●      Complications of hemorrhage, perforation, or obstruction

●      Initially diagnosed by intestinal resection at time of acute abdomen

●      ∼ 50% of patients require laparotomy for complications of hemorrhage, perforation, or obstruction

Microscopic features of MEITL

           

●      Transmural, dense lymphocytic infiltrate

●      Lymphoma cells small to medium-sized and round

●      Dark nuclei and pale cytoplasm

●      Minimal inflammatory background

●      Adjacent mucosa often shows intraepithelial lymphocytes

 


MEITL immunophenotype?

 

●      CD3(+), CD8(+), CD56(+), TCR-γδ(+) or TCR-β(+), CD4(-)

●      Monoclonal T-cell receptor gene rearrangements

●      Chromosomal gain of 9q34 or deletions within 16q12.1 (23% of cases)

MEITL top DDx         

 

●      Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma

●      Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified

●      Extranodal NK-/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type

●      Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma

●      ALK(-) anaplastic large cell lymphoma
           

 

*HSTCL Hepatosplenic T-cell Lymphoma

 

Define Hepatosplenic T-Cell Lymphoma

  

●      Clinically aggressive extranodal and systemic T-cell lymphoma

●      Spleen, liver, and bone marrow involvement


What % of NHL is Hepatosplenic T-Cell Lymphoma

 

●      Rare

●      < 1% of all non-Hodgkin lymphomas

Age group affected by Hepatosplenic T-Cell Lymphoma

        

●      Young adults

●      Median age: 35 years

●      Following solid organ transplant or Crohn's

Clinical presentation of Hepatosplenic T-Cell Lymphoma

   

●      B symptoms

●      Massive splenomegaly; common hepatomegaly

●      Minimal or absent peripheral lymphadenopathy

Prognosis of Hepatosplenic T-Cell Lymphoma

        

●      Poor prognosis

Distribution of disease in spleen?

         

●      Red pulp cords and sinuses

Distribution of disease in BM?          

 

●      Bone marrow and liver: Sinusoids




●      Image: IHC for CD3 highlights HSTCL cells that are expanding sinuses in a mostly linear pattern in the bone marrow


Cytological features of Hepatosplenic T-Cell Lymphoma

 

●      Lymphoma cells small to intermediate in size

●      Clear cytoplasm, devoid of azurophilic granules

●      Occasional cases with blastoid morphology

Nonlymphoid cells in Hepatosplenic T-Cell Lymphoma commonly have what features      

 

●      Mild to moderate dyspoietic features

●      Not associated with specific cytopenias or MDS-related cytogenetic aberrancies

Hepatosplenic T-Cell Lymphoma typical immunophenotype?

 

●      CD3(+), CD4(-), CD8(-/+), CD5(-), CD56(+), TCR-γδ(+)

○      Non-activated cytotoxic cells: TIA1(+), granzyme M (+), granzyme-B (-)

●      Subset of cases express TCR-αβ

○      Similar clinicopathologic and cytogenetic features to TCR-γδ(+) cases


Is Hepatosplenic T-Cell Lymphoma typical a CD4 or CD8 positive T cell lymphoma?  

 

●      CD4(-)

●      CD8(-/+)

●      Typically double negative


What TCR does Hepatosplenic T-Cell Lymphoma have?  

 

●      TCR-γδ(+) gamma delta

●      Subset of cases express TCR-αβ

●      Similar clinicopathologic and cytogenetic features to TCR-γδ(+) cases

Mutations seen in Hepatosplenic T-Cell lymphoma?         

 

●      Isochromosome 7q in ∼ 50% of cases

●      Trisomy 8 in ∼ 70% of cases by FISH

●      Mutations in SETD2, INO80, TET3, SMARCA2, PIK3CD, STAT5B, and STAT3 genes

●      Other less common driver mutations reported in TP53, UBR5, and IDH2 genes

HSTCL Top Differential Diagnoses

        

●      T-LGLL

●      T-PLL

●      ANKL

●      Nonsplenic cytotoxic T-cell lymphoma with γδ(+) phenotype

*Anaplastic large cell lymphoma (in blood and bone marrow)

ALK+ ALCL Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma

 

Define ALK+ Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (ALCL)

 

●      CD30(+) systemic lymphoma of T-cell or T-null lineage with chromosomal abnormalities involving 2p23/anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)

●      T-cell lymphoma consisting of lymphoid cells that are usually large with abundant cytoplasm and pleomorphic, often horseshoe-shaped nuclei, with a translocation involving the ALK gene and expression of ALK protein, and expression of CD30

 


What is ALK?  

 

●      Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) → enzyme encoded by the ALK gene

●      aka ALK tyrosine kinase receptor or CD246



3 ways the ALK gene can be oncogenic?

 

●      1) By forming a fusion gene with any of several other genes

●      2) By gaining additional gene copies

●      3) Through mutations of the DNA code for the gene itself

What general age groups may be affected by ALK+ ALCL?

 

●      Children and adults (Dr Medeiros: younger patients)

●      Male predominance

Most ALK+ ALCL patients present with early or advanced clinical stage?

●      Clinical stage III/IV (advanced)

Is extranodal involvement rare or common in ALK+ ALCL?  

 

●      Yes - common (60%)

ALK+ ALCL 5-year survival?

 

●      Good 5-year survival: *80-90%*


ALK+ ALCL Microscopic Pathology: Characteristic cells? 

 

●      *"Hallmark cells"* characteristic (horseshoe, kidney shape)

○      Large; eccentric horseshoe-/kidney-shaped nuclei

○      Prominent paranuclear eosinophilic Golgi region

○      The typical comma shaped or indented “hallmark cell” is a key feature and helpful diagnostic clue.

●      Infiltration of lymph nodes with a sinusoidal pattern of involvement can be seen.

 

 

ASH image bank

 

 

Blood journal


Do neoplastic cells grow singly or cohesively?   

 

●      Neoplastic cells grow cohesively & preferentially involve the sinuses


How many morphologic patterns of ALK+ ALCL are there?    

 

●      4 (WHO 2016)

4 morphologic patterns of ALK+ ALCL?   

 

●      1) "Common or classic pattern" - 80%

●      2) "Lymphohistiocytic pattern" (5-10%)

○      Tumour cells admixed with reactive histiocytes

●      3) "Small cell pattern" (5-10%)

○      "Fried egg cells", signet ring-like cells (rare), Hallmark cells (always)

●      4) "Sarcomatoid" (1%)

●      Note, WHO 2008 described "Hodgkin-like pattern"(3%)

○      Mimicking nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma (NSHL)

○      This was probably what's now called "sarcomatoid"?

2 important positive IHC stains for ALK+ ALCL diagnosis?

 

●      ALK: positive

●      CD30: strongly and uniformly positive

●      Both needed to confirm the Dx

 



ALK+ ALCL Immunophenotype:

 

●      CD30 is uniformly and strongly positive

●      CD3 - in 75%

●      CD2, CD4, CD5 usually positive (70%)

●      Aberrant T-cell immunophenotype common

○      Loss of CD3, CD5, and T-cell receptors

●      Expression of cytotoxic molecules in 50%

○      Positive for TIA1, granzyme-B, perforin

●      EMA ++

 

ALK+ ALCL most frequent chromosomal translocation?

 

●      t(2;5)(p23;q35)*, detected in 75%

●      Involves the ALK gene (chr 2)

●      ALK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase) gene (chr 2)

●      NPM (nucleophosmin) gene (chr 5)

●      Product of the *NPM-ALK* fusion gene is oncogenic

 

What are the other chromosomal translocations

 

●      inv(2)

●      t(1;2) (TPM3 - ALK)

 

ALK+ ALCL Top Differential Diagnoses? 

 

●      Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (CHL)

○      HRS cells, CD30+

●      DLBCL expressing CD30

●      Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, NOS

●      ALK(-) ALCL

●      Primary cutaneous ALCL


Anti-CD30 drug for ALCL?   

 

●      Brentuximab vedotin mab-drug conjugate

 

Caveats and Pearls

·       Some cases have null-cell phenotype, lacking expression of all T-cell markers

ALK- ALCL Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma

 

Define ALK(-) Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (ALCL)

 

●      Lymphoma that histologically resembles ALK(+) anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL)

●      CD30(+)

●      Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) is absent

●      ALCL with comparable morphologic/histologic and phenotypic features to ALK+ ALCL, but lacking ALK rearrangement and the ALK protein

How does prognosis of ALK(-) ALCL compare to that of ALK(+) ALCL?

 

●      Poorer prognosis than ALK(+) ALCL

●      Hence one of the reasons the distinction is important

How does prognosis of ALK(-) ALCL compare to that of PTCL-NOS?

 

●      Better prognosis than PTCL-NOS

3 subsets of ALK(-) ALCL

 

●      ∼ 30% with translocations of 6p25.3/DUSP22

○      Good prognosis similar to patients with ALK(+) ALCL

●      ∼ 8% with translocations of 3q28/TP63

○      Patients have very poor prognosis

○      Can do immunostain → positivity doesn’t necessarily mean the translocation is present. Could use as a screen, if positive → send for FISH

●      Remaining cases double negative

○      Patients have intermediate prognosis


What subset of ALK(-) ALCL has a good prognosis similar to that of ALK(+) ALCL?

     

●      The ∼ 30% with *translocations of 6p25.3/DUSP22*

●      Good prognosis similar to patients with ALK(+) ALCL

What subset of ALK(-) ALCL has the worst prognosis

 

●      ∼ 8% with translocations of 3q28/TP 63

●      Patients have very poor prognosis

ALK(-) Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (ALCL) Features of Microscopic Pathology

     

●      Most common variant closely mimics classical variant of ALK(+) ALCL:

○      ALK(+) ALCL: T-cell lymphoma consisting of lymphoid cells that are usually large with abundant cytoplasm and pleomorphic, often horseshoe-shaped nuclei, showing strong uniform expression of *CD30*

○      Often more cytologically anaplastic and less hallmark cells than ALK(+) ALCL

○      Cohesive growth pattern; often sinusoidal involvement

 

What are the cytological differences between ALK(-) and ALK(+) ALCL? 

 

●      Hallmark cells less frequently seen in ALK(-) ALCL than ALK(+) ALCL

●      ALK(-) ALCL often more anaplastic than ALK(+) ALCL



ALK(-) ALCL DUSP22 rearranged cases show what cytological features?    

 

●      Sheet-like growth, less pleomorphic than other cases of ALK(-) ALCL

●      Doughnut cells common


Eosinophils may be present in ALK(-) ALCL and when present you must consider what alternative Dx?         

 

●      CHL


What disease associated cell type is seen in this case of ALK(+) ALCL?  

 



Morphological appearance of anaplastic large cell lymphoma: large anaplastic, neoplastic cells.

 

●      The arrow indicates typical *hallmark tumor cells* with lobulated nuclei

●      Also described as horse-shoe or reniform (kidney) like

ALK(-) ALCL Ancillary Tests?   

 

●      Immunophenotypic studies needed to confirm dx

●      Monoclonal T-cell receptor gene rearrangements

Name 2 EBV IHC stains

 

●      EBER

●      LMP1

Classic ALK(-) ALCL immunophenotype

 

●      CD30 is uniformly and strongly positive

●      ALK(-) ALCL expresses at least 1 T-cell antigen such as

○      CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD43, CD45RO, and T-cell receptors

●      Aberrant T-cell immunophenotype common

○      Loss of CD3, CD5, and T-cell receptors

●      Expression of cytotoxic molecules in 50%

○      Lack of expression doesn't exclude Dx (TIA1, granzyme-B, perforin)

●      Clusterin usually positive

●      CD15(-/+), Bcl-2(+/-)

●      Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) latent membrane protein 1 (LMP1) (-)

●      CD45 usually (+) by flow cytometry


Absent expression of T-cell markers is called "___-____" type in ALK(-) ALCL   

 

●       "Null-cell" type

What IHC marker is useful to differentiate from CD30 + CHL?     

 

●      PAX5

●      Positive in CHL

●      Negative in ALK-ALCL

Top Differential Diagnoses

 

●      ALK(+) ALCL

●      PTCL-NOS

●      CHL

●      Cutaneous ALCL

○      Staging studies needed to establish diagnosis of cutaneous ALCL

●      Breast implant-associated ALCL

○      Localized lymphoma arising in capsule surrounding breast implant

 

Anti-CD30 drug for ALCL?

 

●      Brentuximab vedotin

 

Caveats and Pearls

●      Some cases with null-cell phenotype, lacking expression of all T-cell markers

Breast-implant Associated ALCL Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma

 

 

What is Breast Implant-Associated Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (BI-ALCL)     

  

●      ALCL of T-/null-cell lineage that arises around breast implants and is ALK(-)
Provisional entity in 2016 WHO update


What is the likely parthenogenesis of BI-ALCL - what types of breast implants are implicated? 

 

●      Unknown - The carcinogenic factors or mechanisms are not identified in BI-ALCL

●      Occurs with textured saline and silicone-filled implants

●      Pathogenesis likely related with texturing process

 

What are the possible pathogenetic mechanisms ?  

 

●      Implant contents or implant texturing process

○      No bona fide cases of BI-ALCL associated with smooth implants, only with with *textured* saline and silicone-filled implants

●      Autoimmune-mediated cytokines

●      Biofilm bacteria on surface of textured implants:Ralstonia spp.

○      Chronic antigenic stimulation of T lymphocytes is likely

●      Activating mutations of JAK1 and STAT3 in subset of cases

ALK(-) ALCL accounts for > ____% of lymphomas associated with breast implants

     

●      >90% BI-ALCL

 

How long after the implant is placed is the tumor usually detected   

 

●      A number of years after implant (median: 8 years)


How do patients with BI-ALCL present?

   

●      ∼ 70% of patients present with effusion

●      ∼ 30% of patients present with tumor mass, ± effusion


Treatment for BI-ALCL  

 

●      Complete surgical removal of capsule and implant lead to optimal disease-free survival and overall survival

●      Adjuvant chemo with CHOP

●      Immunotherapy with anti-CD30 Brentuximab vedotin for progressive or refractory cases (occurs in subset of cases)

2 best imaging modalities for BI-ALCL?  

 

●      US most sensitive modality to detect effusion around implant

●      PET/CT most sensitive to detect and follow tumor mass or recurrence

Microscopic features of BI-ALCL

 

●      Fibrinonecrotic material on luminal side of capsule where individual cells or tumor cell clusters are contained

●      Fibrinoid layer subtly merges with surrounding fibrous tissue to appear as thick capsule

●      Cells are large, pleomorphic with abundant cytoplasm

●      Occasional kidney-shaped nuclei (hallmark cells)
Subset of cases invade beyond capsule into surrounding soft tissue

BI-ALCL immunophenotype?

 

●      CD30(+) with uniform membranous or Golgi pattern

●      T-cell antigens (+); aberrant immunophenotype (+/-)

●      Cytotoxic antigens (Granzyme B, perforin, and TIA-1) (+/-)

●      EMA(+/-), clusterin (+/-)

●      CD45/LCA(+/-)

●      CD15(-/+), ALK(-), B-cell antigens (-), EBV-LMP1(-)

●      Proliferation rate (Ki-67) usually high

●      Monoclonal T-cell receptor gene rearrangements (+)


BI-ALCL top DDx?   

 

●      Primary cutaneous ALCL disseminated to breast

●      ALK(-) and ALK(+) ALCL

●      Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified

 

Nodal T follicular helper cell lymphoma

WHO5 Recommendations for reporting nodal T follicular helper cell lymphomas (nTFHLs)

·       nTFHL-AI may be diagnosed on core or excision biopsies, provided the diagnostic criteria are fulfilled

·       nTFHL-F often overlaps with nTFHL-AI, and its diagnosis is best based on excision biopsies

·       nTFHL-NOS is a diagnosis of exclusion that should be based on excision biopsies only

·       Use of the generic term “nTFHL”, rather than nTFHL-NOS or nTFHL-F, is recommended when the diagnosis is based on core biopsies, to prevent misclassification due to insufficient sampling

·       In the event of a change in morphology from one type to another across multiple biopsies or at relapse, the following comment is recommended: “This is consistent with a morphological variation of the patient’s original nTFHL”

 

*AITL Angioimmunoblastic T-cell Lymphoma

What is Angioimmunoblastic T-cell Lymphoma?

 

●      A nodal T cell lymphoma

●      A peripheral T-cell lymphoma derived from CD4(+) T follicular helper cells (TFH)

●      Prominent proliferation of high endothelial venules and follicular dendritic cells

 

AITL is derived from what cells?

 

●      CD4(+) T follicular helper cells (TFH)

Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma is one of several entities included under what umbrella term?

 

●      "Nodal T-cell lymphomas with TFH phenotype"

 

Key clinical characteristics of Angioimmunoblastic T-cell Lymphoma?  

 

●      Systemic disease

●      Immunodysregulation and immunodeficiency

●      Lymphadenopathy

●      HSM

 

What tissues are involved in AITL?

 

●      Spleen, liver, skin rash (pruritic) and BM are frequently involved

Egs of immunodysregulation in AITL?

 

●      Circulating immune complexes

●      Cold agglutinins with hemolytic anemia,

●      Positive rheumatoid factor and anti-smooth muscle antibodies

●      B cell EBV infection may be consequence of underlying immune dysfunction

AITL tends to present with limited or advanced stage?     

 

●      Advanced stage

 

What are the presenting features of AITL?

 

●      Systemic symptoms

●      Generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, &/or splenomegaly

 

AITL is aggressive or indolent?

 

●      Aggressive

 

What is the Median survival of AITL?

 

●      < 3 years (poor prognosis)


Do AITL patients have skin findings?

 

●      Yes - rash or papules may be present

What are the 2 characteristic lab abnormalities seen in AITL?           

 

●      Hypereosinophilia

●      Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia

●      Anemia

3 AITL LN histologic findings

 

  1. Partial or complete effacement of architecture by neoplastic T cells with clear/pale cytoplasm
  2. Proliferation of arborizing high endothelial venules (HEVs)
  3. Proliferation of follicular dendritic cells (FDCs), esp around high endothelial vessels

 

Cytologic description of AITL cells?

 

●      Small to irregular with clear cytoplasm

AITL immunophenotype?

 

●      CD2(+), CD3(+), CD4(+), CD5(+), CD7+/- (aberrant loss or reduced expression), CD8-, TCR-αβ(+)

●      CD10(+/-), Bcl-6(+/-), CXCL13(+/-), PD-1(+/-), ICOS, CXCR5

●      B immunoblasts (+) in variable numbers [CD30(+)]

 

What are 5 TFH cell-associated markers

 

●      CD10, BCL6, PD-1 (CD279), CXCL13, ICOS, CD200

●      Diagnosis requires at least 2, but preferably 3 to call TFH lymphoma

AITL: Expanded follicular dendritic cell meshworks may be identified using what 4 possible markers?

 

●      CD21, CD23, CD35 and CNA42

●      Usually surrounding high endothelial venules.

AITL: what B cells may be present in incr #s on flow?

 

●      B immunoblasts(+) in variable numbers (CD30(+)

Name 3 additional ancillary tests of use when diagnosing AITL (in addition to histology and IHC)?

 

●      Immunophenotype by FC

●      Monoclonal T-cell receptor rearrangements

●      EBER(+) B cells in ~ 80-90% of cases

●      Neoplastic cells have gene expression profile (GEP) of follicular helper T cells
CD21/23 to demonstrate extrafollicular network of follicular dendritic cells

Is EBV + in AITL?

 

●      Yes, but in only in B cells

●      EBER(+) in ~ 80-90% of cases

●      The neoplastic T cells are EBV negative.

AITL genetic profile

 

  • Frequent mutations in TET2 and DNMT3A
  • Other recurrently mutated genes
    • RHOA and IDH2
  • Fusion genes
    • ICOS::CD28, ITK::SYK, and VAV1 fusions

 

Top DDx for AITL?

 

●      PTCL, NOS

●      THRLBL (AITL with increased large B cell may mimic this)

●      CHL (In AITL, EBV+ RS-like cells (CD30+ immunoblasts) of B-cell lineage may be present)

●      Primary cutaneous CD4+ small/medium T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder

●      EBV+ DLBCL, NOS

●      Viral lymphadenitis or drug reaction (drug reaction, Kimura disease, etc)

 

What are the other nodal T Follicular helper T-cell lymphomas?

 

●      Nodal PTCL with TFH phenotype

●      Follicular T-cell lymphoma

Caveats and Pearls

·       May develop a concomitant B-cell lymphoma

EBV-positive T-cell and NK-cell lymphomas

EBV-positive T-cell and NK-cell lymphoproliferative diseases of childhood

Essential: acute presentation with fever and systemic symptoms; multiorgan infiltration by atypical T cells; EBV positivity; exclusion of known immunodeficiency.

Desirable: clonal TR gene rearrangements; HLH; hepatosplenomegaly.

 

What is the 2016 classification of EBV-positive T-cell and NK-cell proliferations        

 

CAEBV = chronic active EBV infection.
