4 subgroups of EBV-positive T-cell and NK-cell lymphoproliferative diseases of childhood described in 2016 WHO

 

  1. Systemic
    1. Systemic EBV-positive T-cell lymphoma of childhood
    2. Chronic active EBV infection of T- and NK-cell type, systemic form
  2. Cutaneous
    1. Hydroa vacciniforme-like lymphoproliferative disorder (Cutaneous CAEBV)
    2. Severe mosquito bite allergy (Cutaneous CAEBV)

Q. EBV-associated T-cell and NK-cell lymphoproliferative disorders in the paediatric age group can be categorized into two major groups:   

 

●      1) Systemic EBV-positive T cell lymphoma of childhood

●      2) Chronic active EBV infection.

Q. Both Systemic EBV-positive T cell lymphoma of childhood  & CAEBV occur with increased frequency in what 2 ethnic groups?   

 

●      Asians and in Native Americans from Central and South America and Mexico.

Q. Systemic EBV-positive T-cell lymphoma of childhood has a very fulminant clinical course, usually associated with what syndrome?

 

●      HLH: a hemophagocytic syndrome

Q. Chronic active EBV infection of T- and NK cell type shows a broad range of clinical manifestations; give 2 egs of indolent localized forms

 

●      Hydroa vacciniforme-like lymphoproliferative disorder

●      Severe mosquito bite allergy

 

What is “severe mosquito bite allergy”?

 

●      EBV positive NK-cell lymphoproliferative disorder characterized by →  high fever and intense local skin symptoms, including erythema, bullae, ulcers, skin necrosis,
and deep scarring following mosquito bites.

●      Patients have NK-cell lymphocytosis in the peripheral blood and an increased
risk of developing

○      Hemophagocytic syndrome

○      Progressing into overt NK/T-cell lymphoma or aggressive NK-cell leukaemia in the longstanding clinical course.

 

 

ENKTL Extranodal NK-/T-cell Lymphoma, Nasal Type

Essential: infiltration of extranodal tissues by lymphoma cells with variable morphology; NK- or cytotoxic T-cell phenotype; majority of tumour cells positive for EBER.

Desirable: angiocentric growth and necrosis.

 

What is Extranodal NK-/T-cell Lymphoma, Nasal Type?

 

●      Predominantly extranodal lymphoma of either natural killer-cell (NK) or T-cell lineage

 

What are the key features of NK/T-Cell Nasal type?

 

●      Characterized by necrosis, cytotoxic immunophenotype, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection

●      Vascular/angio destruction is common

 

What infectious agent is associated with NK/T Cell Lymphoma Nasal type?

 

●      Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection



Simplistically, Extranodal NK-/T-cell Lymphoma, Nasal Type can be divided into what 2 types?

 

●      Nasal or extranasal

Nasal cases are usually defined as?

 

●      Neoplasm involving → upper aerodigestive tract

●      Nasal cavity, nasopharynx, paranasal sinuses, palate

●      Regional lymphadenopathy occurs in 10-20% of patients

Extranasal cases are usually defined as?

 

●      Neoplasm involving any site (other than nasal primary)

●      Skin is most common extranasal site

 

Most common extranasal site of Extranodal NK-/T-cell Lymphoma, Nasal Type?

           

●      Skin

How common is BM involvement by Extranodal NK-/T-cell Lymphoma, Nasal Type?

 

●      10-20%* of patients

 

Extranodal NK-/T-cell Lymphoma, Nasal Type may be misinterpreted as?

 

●      Cytologic spectrum of nasal-type extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma is wide

●      Small cell neoplasms can be misinterpreted as → chronic inflammation

●      Necrosis and superimposed acute and *chronic inflammation* can lead to incorrect diagnosis

●      Old term → “lethal midline granuloma”


What histologic finding may be helpful to support diagnosis?

 

●      Angiocentricity and angiodestruction are helpful findings but are not constant
Most likely to be absent in small biopsy specimens



Histologic features of Extranodal NK-/T-cell Lymphoma, Nasal Type?

 

●      Wide cytologic spectrum

●      Angiocentricity and angiodestruction

●      Necrosis and superimposed acute and chronic inflammation (which can lead to incorrect diagnosis)

 

Extranodal NK-/T-cell Lymphoma - What % are NK cell lineage?

 

●      Approximately 2/3 of tumors

 

NK cell lineage immunophenotype?

 

·       CD2(+), cyt CD3-ε(+), CD56(+/-), CD5(-), CD8(-), TCR gene rearrangements(-)

 

T cell lineage immunophenotype?

 

·       CD2(+), CD3-ε(+), CD5(+), CD8(+/-), TCR-β (βF1)(+), TIA1(+), GZM-B(+), perforin (+), CD56(-/+)

 

What is the most typical immunophenotype for Extranodal NK-/T-cell Lymphoma, Nasal Type?

 

Most typical:

-        CD2+, CD5-, CD56+

-        CD7 variable

-        sCD3 negative (because they are NK cells)

-        cCD3 epsilon+

-        CD43 and 45RO often+

-        Other T cell & NK cell associated antigens including CD4, 8, 16 and 57 are usually -

-        Cytotoxic markers +: granzyme, perforin & TIA

-        HLADR, CD25, FAS & FASL commonly expressed

-        CD30+ in 30%


Which of the following lineages may have TCR gene rearrangements NK cell lineage or cytotoxic lineage?

 

●      Cytotoxic T cells

●      NOT seen in NK cells

What % are cytotoxic T-cell lineage?

 

●      Approximately 1/3 of tumors

●      True T-cell lineage in ~ 25-35% of cases

 

Cytotoxic T-cell lineage immunophenotype?

 

●      CD2(+), CD3-e(+), CD5(+), CD8(+/-), TCR-β(βF1)(+), TCR gene rearrangements(+)

●      TIA1(+), GZM-B(+), perforin (+), CD56(-/+)

Regardless of NK vs cytotoxic T cell lineage, all tumors are positive for (2)?

 

●      Cytotoxic proteins

●      EBV (best shown by in situ hybridization for EBER)


3 cytotoxic proteins?

 

-        TIA, GZM-B, perforin


Extranodal NK-/T-cell Lymphoma, Nasal Type Top Differential Diagnoses?

 

●      Cytotoxic EBV-peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified

●      B-cell lymphomas involving upper aerodigestive tract (usually DLBCL)

●      Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly called Wegener's)

 

 

Other PTCL

*PTCL, NOS (Peripheral T-cell Lymphoma)

 

What are the 5 nodal T cell lymphomas?

 

●      PTCL, NOS

●      AITL

●      ATLL, HTLV-1(+)

●      ALK(+) ALCL

●      ALK(-) ALCL

 

Define the PTCL, NOS

 

●      Mature T-cell lymphomas that cannot be classified into specific T-cell categories

●      Heterogeneous group in current WHO classification

●      PTCL is, in part, diagnosis of exclusion

PTCL represents approximately ____% of all non-Hodgkin lymphomas

 

●      6.0%

Does PTCL, NOS occur in children or adults?

 

●      Mainly arises in middle-aged or older adults; rare in children

Does PTCL, NOS typically presents as limited stage disease    

 

●      NO! Advanced-stage disease with B symptoms

●      Lymphadenopathy; extranodal sites often involved

 

PTCL, NOS prognosis?

 

●      Poor prognosis with frequent relapses

●      Management with combination chemotherapy ± consolidation therapy

●      Response to therapy is poor; frequent relapses

Microscopic description of classic PTCL, NOS?

 

●      Paracortical infiltrate or diffuse effacement of lymph node architecture

●      Wide cytological spectrum

●      Background inflammatory cells often numerous

●      ± postcapillary venules in arborizing fashion

●      ± high rates of proliferation and apoptosis

PTCL, NOS immunophenotype?

 

●      Pan-T-cell antigens (+)

●      CD4(+) CD8(-) or less often CD4(-) CD8(+)

●      Aberrant T-cell immunophenotypes in ∼ 80% of cases

●      CD30 can be (+), exceptionally CD15(+)

●      Cytotoxic molecules (+/-)

●      Aberrant T-cell immunophenotypes in ∼ 80% of cases

●      Loss or deletion of 1 or more pan-T-cell antigens

●      Rarely B-cell antigens are aberrantly expressed

●      Can express B-cell antigens: rare: CD20 and or CD79a most frequent


How common are aberrant T-cell immunophenotypes in PTCL, NOS?

   

●      ~ 80% of cases


Why might you confuse PTCL, NOS with ALCL or Hodgkins?  

 

●      CD30 can be positive, exceptionally CD15(+)


PTCL shows monoclonal _______ gene rearrangements

 

●      TCR

○      Monoclonal TRB &/or TRG rearrangements

 

PTCL, NOS DDx?

 

●      Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma

●      Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma

●      Anaplastic large cell lymphoma

●      Classic Hodgkin lymphoma

●      T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma

●      Mycosis fungoides involving lymph node

●      Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma

●      Extranodal NK-/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type

 

Differential diagnosis of peripheral T-cell lymphoma NOS (WHO5)

Disease

Clinicopathological features

Molecular/genetic findings

Nodal TFH cell lymphoma, angioimmunoblastic type

Distinctive clinical syndromea

FDC hyperplasia (CD21/CD23), polymorphous inflammatory infiltrate, arborizing HEVs, EBV+/− B immunoblasts

CD4+; expression of two or more TFH markers (CD10, BCL6, PD1, CXCL13, CXCR5, ICOS, SAP)

RHOA p.G17V and IDH2 p.R172 mutations; lack of deletions of CDKN2A and PTEN; rare TP53 deletions and/or mutations

Nodal TFH cell lymphoma NOS

CD4+; expression of two or more TFH markers (CD10, BCL6, PD1, CXCL13, CXCR5, ICOS, SAP)

Lack of hyperplasia of FDCs and HEVs

RHOA p.G17V mutations in a subset; lack of deletions of CDKN2A and PTEN; rare TP53 deletions and/or mutations

ALK− anaplastic large cell lymphoma

Large anaplastic (hallmark) cells, cohesive growth pattern, sinusoidal involvement

CD30+ (strong and uniform); EMA+; cytotoxic granules+/−, CD4+/−; CD3−/+; CD43+; PAX5−; reduced T-cell surface antigen expression

DUSP22 rearrangements (can also occur in PTCL-NOS); JAK-1 and STAT3 activation

Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma

Mostly geographically restricted to areas in which HTLV-1 is endemic; hypercalcaemia; simultaneous opportunistic infections

Presence of “flower cells”

CD4+, CD25+, CD7−, CD30−/+, CCR4+, FOXP3−/+

Positive serological studies for HTLV-1; positive HTLV-1 integration studies; CCR4 mutations and IRF4 amplifications

EBV-positive nodal T- and NK-cell lymphoma

EBER positivity in most of the tumour cells

Cytotoxic phenotype; CD56− (usually)

Positive TR gene rearrangements (cases with T-cell lineage); negative TR gene rearrangements (cases with NK-cell lineage)

Classic Hodgkin lymphoma

HRS cells in background of reactive T cells with normal phenotypic profile

Negative TR gene rearrangements / polyclonal T cells

T-cell/histiocyte–rich large B-cell lymphoma

Large CD20+ blasts in background of reactive T cells with normal phenotypic profile

Negative TR gene rearrangements / polyclonal T cells

Nodal marginal zone lymphoma

Neoplastic cells are B cells (CD20+); these small/medium-sized cells usually grow around follicles and into the interfollicular areas

Positive IG gene rearrangements

Paracortical hyperplasia

Expansion of T cells with normal phenotypic profile with mixed CD4 and CD8 populations; variable CD30 expression

Negative TR gene rearrangements / polyclonal T cells

 

What somatic mutations can occur in PTCL-NOS?

 

●      TP53, PRDM1, PTEN, CDKN2A/CDKN2B, STAT3, and MYC alterations associated with PTCL-GATA3 subgroup

●      TET1, TET3, and DNMT3A mutations associated with PTCL-TBX21 molecular subgroup

 

What translocation may be seen in a subset of patients with PTCL, NOS?

 

●      t(5;9)(q33;q22); more common in PTCL with TFH immunophenotype

●      t(5;9)(q33;q22) ITK/SYK

 

Additional questions

Q. What 4 IHCs are used to define the 2 subgroups of PTCL-NOS?

·       TBX21 (20% cutoff)

·       CXCR3 (20% cutoff)

·       GATA3 (50% cutoff)

·       CCR4 (50% cutoff)

·       If TBX21(+) &/or CXCR3(+): TBX21 subgroup

·       If TBX21(-), CXCR3(-), GATA3(+), &/or CCR4(+): GATA3 subgroup

·       If all 4 antibodies negative: Unclassified

·        

Q. Which group is associated with poorer prognosis?

GATA3

Caveats and Pearls

• PTCL, NOS is a diagnosis of exclusion
